title: High availability: single point of failure, redundancy and failover

videos.script: A web shop has two load balancers and three web servers. The owner calls it redundant. {{shop}} Then the one line to the internet goes down, and the shop is gone, with five healthy machines behind it. {{line}} High availability is not about how many machines you have. It is about what happens when one of them stops. {{stops}} In this lesson you put a number on availability, the famous nines, and see how little downtime each nine allows. {{nines}} You work out why a chain of parts is weaker than its weakest link. And why two parts side by side are so much stronger than one. {{chain}} Then you look at the lab's own data centre and find the parts that have no twin. {{spof}} You also see what failover really costs. A machine has to notice, decide and switch, and each of those takes time. {{timeline}} Set the timers too tight and a healthy pair flips back and forth. Cut the wrong cable and both machines decide they are in charge. {{split}} Lessons 15 and 16 build the redundancy and measure the gaps. This lesson is the arithmetic that says where to put it. {{end}}
